question: A patient at the end of a 90-minute laparoscopic cholecystectomy opens eyes to command, squeezes your hand, and lifts her head for >5 seconds. Neuromuscular blockade was reversed 10 minutes ago. SpO₂ is 99% on 40% O₂. What is the most appropriate next action?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Extubation in the supine position risks aspiration; head-up or lateral position is preferred, and coughing/swallowing should be confirmed.

answers.text: Extubate when the patient is breathing regularly, following commands, with protective reflexes intact, in a semi-recumbent or lateral position

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Safe extubation criteria are met: consciousness (follows commands), adequate muscle power (head lift >5s), intact reflexes (coughing/swallowing), and adequate oxygenation. Lateral or head-up position reduces aspiration risk.

answers.text: Wait for train-of-four ratio >0.9 before extubating despite clinical signs of recovery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Clinical criteria for extubation are already met; waiting indefinitely for TOF >0.9 when full reversal signs are present delays care unnecessarily — though TOF monitoring is a useful adjunct.

answers.text: Administer a further dose of neostigmine before extubation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The patient already shows full clinical reversal (head lift, command following). Repeat neostigmine is unnecessary and risks cholinergic excess (bradycardia, bronchospasm).

overallFeedback.feedback: Extubate when the patient follows commands, holds head lift >5 seconds, has protective reflexes, and is in a head-up or lateral position — all these criteria are satisfied in this case.
Excellent. Safe extubation = consciousness + adequate ventilation + protective reflexes + muscle power (head lift >5s) + optimal positioning. All criteria are met here.
